title: On culture and toxic leadership
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Returning to school leadership after four years away, Hughes reflects on what unites the best schools she has visited worldwide: a strong, shared sense of culture and intellectual curiosity among staff. She cites UCL research showing NPQ impact depends on being embedded in supportive school cultures, and draws on her work with the Teaching Commission investigating teacher retention, which identified toxic leadership and staff infantilisation as major drivers of attrition. In the piece's most striking section, Hughes discloses her own decade-long experience of workplace bullying by a former leader - including manipulation, public humiliation and a period of suicidal ideation - and frames it as evidence that toxic leadership is common and too often quietly tolerated in schools. She closes with five practical strategies (defined core values, distributed leadership, transparent communication, alignment with agency, psychological safety) for proactively building cultures resistant to toxic leadership.
points: Hughes's disclosure of surviving sustained workplace bullying, including a period of suicidal ideation, grounds her leadership argument in lived testimony rather than abstract theory.
She cites the Teaching Commission's finding that toxic leadership and staff infantilisation are major drivers pushing experienced, highly skilled career-changer teachers out of the profession.
Her observation that toxic leaders are frequently 'moved on' rather than removed - sometimes reassigned by dioceses - names a specific institutional failure mode that perpetuates harm across schools.

Her five-part framework (values, distributed leadership, transparent communication, alignment with agency, psychological safety) offers leaders concrete, actionable levers against toxic culture, not just diagnosis.
quotes: The research highlights that school culture significantly impacts teachers' and leaders' perceptions of workload. Workload isn't merely about hours worked but also its complexity and meaningfulness.

One of the big factors we have found is driving teachers out of school is toxic leadership and teachers being infantilised. They were horrified with the way they were patronised and infantilised when they qualified and began to teach.
From midnight emails telling me that data was needed at 8:30am the next morning to screaming at me like a child in their office, there wasn't really a day where I wasn't in tears.
I was close to suicide. One weekend... I realised I couldn't take it much more and when I started to think of ways I could kill myself causing the least fuss to my family, I knew I had to get out.

Toxic leadership can erode trust, stifle intellectual curiosity and fracture teams in schools. However, fostering a healthy school culture can serve as a buffer against these detrimental leadership behaviours.
